name: Open Source & Self-Hosted Models
intro:
Open source and self-hosted models covers the software stack for running AI under an organization's own infrastructure: frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow and Keras), serving engines (vLLM, llama.cpp), local runners (Ollama), and the distribution layer (Hugging Face Transformers and its hub). It excludes hosted API products from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google covered elsewhere on this site. The defining trait is that the organization controls the weights, the inference environment, and the data path, with no vendor between model and request.

A buyer here is choosing a serving strategy more than a single product. PyTorch and TensorFlow/Keras sit upstream as the frameworks models get built and fine-tuned in, with PyTorch now the default for new releases. vLLM is the pick for high-throughput, multi-GPU production serving. llama.cpp targets lightweight, CPU-capable, edge and offline use. Ollama wraps llama.cpp into the simplest path to a working local model on one machine. Hugging Face Transformers and its hub cut across all of these as the place models get published and pulled from.

The landscape shifted in the last year. OpenAI released gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b under Apache 2.0 in August 2025, its first open-weight models in years, giving self-hosted setups a frontier-adjacent option beyond Meta or Mistral weights. Hugging Face contributed Safetensors to the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026, formalizing a secure, non-executable format as the supply chain standard, alongside vLLM, now itself a Foundation project.

The clearest reference points are vLLM for production-scale serving, Ollama for the fastest route to a working local model, and Hugging Face Transformers as the provenance layer most other tools here depend on.

reading.body:
Organizations can run AI models entirely on their own hardware using six major open-source tools, avoiding vendor lock-in and external data transmission.

Self-hosted inference has become viable at scale. Ollama and llama.cpp allow local model execution with minimal infrastructure. vLLM handles high-throughput workloads on self-owned hardware. PyTorch and TensorFlow provide the frameworks for training and deployment pipelines. Hugging Face operates as the central model registry, though it introduces a supply-chain dependency. The common thread across all six is elimination of data upload to external inference APIs.

For AI scaling specifically, this matters because compute that runs locally does not require network bandwidth to cloud providers, and models can be deployed to edge hardware, data centers, or on-premises clusters without vendor approval. This shifts the constraint from cloud capacity to building space, power provisioning, and cooling at the deployment site. Organizations can now bind their AI spending directly to their own infrastructure investments rather than cloud pricing.

What this collection does not cover: production governance, model verification, or how to validate that downloaded models have not been poisoned or modified. The data flags "model provenance tracking" and "supply-chain verification needed" as known gaps, not solved problems. Likewise, cost of deployment, throughput benchmarks, and scaling limits for each tool are absent. The page establishes that self-hosting is possible, not that it is optimal for any specific workload.
